utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Moskowitz, before we start, do you mind if I, first of all, thank Mr. Krajina for kindly drawing our attention yesterday to the need to put the record straight. Actually, I checked the transcript, which I got this morning, and it is not very clear what the witness said about Vlatko Kupreskic. Actually, in English, it is very clear that you have the feeling that he said that he saw Vlatko Kupreskic. So I think, again, Mr. Krajina is right, we should probably put it straight, and I wonder whether Mr. Moskowitz could ask a question at this point to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and, in fact, at the break yesterday afternoon, after hearing from Mr. Krajina, I spoke briefly with the witness, and he immediately said that he had simply misspoken and wanted to make the record straight, and so we intend to do that first thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ahmic, you told me yesterday that you wanted to set the record straight on a misstatement that you had made about Vlatko Kupreskic. Essentially, you said that while you were in the ditch on April 16th, 1993, and you were seeing various waves of soldiers coming through Ahmici, that two of those soldiers you recognised in particular, Blazo Tutic and Safradin Ivica, and that you said that they had some sort of relationship with Vlatko Kupreskic. Now, let me ask you. Did you, in fact, see Vlatko Kupreskic at that time in Ahmici while you were in the ditch?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I made a mistake. I mentioned Vlatko Kupreskic. It's on the record. I was thinking of Zoran and Miro Kupreskic because they were working in Masinogradnja, the factory where I used to work. I didn't see Vlatko that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me further clarify. You are not saying and you did not mean to say that you saw Vlatko, Zoran, or Mirjan that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. I only said that they used to work with the two men I saw. They used to work in that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So you were merely saying that these two people, Blazo Tutic and Safradin Ivica, were co-workers with Zoran and Mirjan, and your mistake was that you had said that they were co-workers with Vlatko. That's what you intended to convey yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And we do apologise for that mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I also want to clarify and make sure we have clear on the record one other thing that you testified to yesterday, and this is an incident that occurred the night before, on April 15, 1993, when you were at your uncle Sakib's house and you were walking out of his house that evening to return to your home when you overheard a conversation between Ivo Papic and his son Dragan Papic. Please tell us, at approximately what time in the evening you overheard that conversation between those two people?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was at about 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That would be on July 15th, 1993 -- I'm sorry, April 15th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point, I would ask the usher's assistance in handing a series of photographs to Mr. Ahmic in the order that I'm presenting them to the usher so that he can briefly identify the photographs and tell us about them in a manner that might illustrate his testimony of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, Exhibit 28 is now on the machine next to you. Could you briefly tell us what that shows?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It shows the mosque in the lower village of Ahmici before the attack on the 28th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So that's the way the mosque looked before it was damaged in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can we have the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what that shows? This is Exhibit 29.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This shows the damaged mosque after the attack on the 28th of October, and the greatest damage was at the top, and this was done, as we learned from Croatian services, by Nenad Santic, who shot from a gun from Zume -- recoilless gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe you referred to the attack in October --

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can we have the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before we remove that photograph. Does this picture portray the entire damage done to the minaret during the attack in October 1992, or was there more damage done that this picture does not show?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was more damage, as I've already said. The top was damaged and some roof tiles were broken, but you can't see that from this angle. It is probably on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: The minaret in October 1992 was not taken down, though, was it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Was this damage that you see and the other damage that you've described repaired between the two attacks, between 1992 and the attack in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Exhibit number 30 shows, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This shows the house of Dragan Papic and Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that before the attack in April of '93, you witnessed an anti-aircraft gun on the back of a truck in the vicinity of the Papic house and that you saw Dragan Papic on that truck using the weapon, and could you point for us where you saw that anti-aircraft gun in relation to the Papic house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was here, in this yard. This is where the road passes, and it was here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You're pointing to an area alongside the Papic house looking like the driveway area of the Papic house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, this is Exhibit 31. For the benefit of the Court, it is a blow-up area of the large map, focusing now in Ahmici on what Colonel Watters described as the turnaround area in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Before we came to court, you placed some circles around some various landmarks and houses in that area, Mr. Ahmic. Are those circles approximately or exactly where you want them to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have a copy, please, of this, Mr. Moskowitz, so we can mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the evidence is given.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, are those circles around the landmarks that you provided us prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, looking at the number 55 on the map, could you tell us, if you can, what house that is?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The house of ^ Sukrija Ahmic which, on the morning of the attack, I saw burning first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether Sukrija was killed during the attack on April 16, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: His wife is ^ Sadeta, is she not?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he had three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: They survived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that his wife's name is Sadeta, but I know that he had three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, turning to the circle marked "J," could you tell us whose house that is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is the house of Ivica Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, before the attack in April of 1993, is that the house where you witnessed materials being loaded and unloaded into that basement of that house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where materials were unloaded into the cellar of that house, yes, that's exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us, to the best of your ability, what kinds of materials you observed being unloaded into the basement of House J, Ivica Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: These were crates, probably wooden crates, quite long, military crates. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did you notice the kind of truck that was being used to unload the crates into the basement of that house, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was quite a big military truck. It was green. It was a military truck with four-wheel drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, across from House J, there's a circle labelled "C." Do you see that? And could you tell us whose house that is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This house belongs to Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And right behind House C is House D, or a circled marked "D." Whose house would that be?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The house belongs to Miro Kupreskic and his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Miro and Zoran, what is their relationship to each other, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you see on this blow-up an area that would correspond to the house of Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it could be here. This is their old house, and this should be Vlatko's new house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You say "their old house." Is that the house that was occupied by Vlatko's father ^ Fanjo?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you take the red marker in front of you and, to the best of your ability, and I know this is a bit of a fuzzy picture, but approximately mark by a circle where you think Vlatko's house is in this photograph or blow-up, Exhibit 31?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: (Marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Finally, there's an area marked "K." Could you tell us what that represents?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It's a warehouse and shop belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, do you see that white area in front of "K," Mr. Ahmic? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Back in 1993, was that white area, in your recollection, as large as it is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Kupreskic levelled the ground with a bulldozer. There used to be a hill there. He destroyed a field belonging to Hazim Ahmic, and he pushed all the soil there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So back in April of 1993, there wasn't such a large white area in front of "K" and in front of Vlatko Kupreskic's house; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, there was only an asphalt road there, and there was a hill there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Finally, before we leave this, has there been, to your knowledge, some additional construction next to the area that you've described as a store, I believe, designated as "K" on this map? Has there been additional construction since April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As I learned, and once I passed through and I saw that probably during the war, a much bigger warehouse had been built, twice as big as the old one, a much bigger warehouse has been built there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If we could now move to the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exhibit number 32 is a photograph, Mr. Ahmic. Do you know this house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is the house belonging to Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exhibit 33 is also a photograph. Could you tell us what that shows, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It shows this is the old warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic and this is the new one, part of the new one. It's much bigger than the old one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, the old warehouse is marked "K" on that blow-up map that we've just looked at. Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exhibit 34 is also a photograph. It shows two houses. Could you identify those houses, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This house belongs to Zoran Kupreskic and this house belongs to Ivica Kupreskic (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you point that out again? I actually missed where you were pointing as you were describing it.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This house belongs to Zoran Kupreskic and this other house belongs to Ivica Kupreskic (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, it was Ivica Kupreskic's house that you observed the unloading of what you believed to be materiel, military materials, prior to the attack in April of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, not shown in this picture is another house behind Zoran Kupreskic's house. It is blocked by Zoran Kupreskic's house. What house is behind Zoran Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The house behind this should be the house of Miro Kupreskic and his father, here behind this house (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, Exhibit 35 now shows a photograph of a house. Whose house is this?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The house belongs to Miro Kupreskic and his father, Ante. They lived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Again, this is the house just behind Zoran's house on that road; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If we can have the ELMO maybe back up a little bit so we can get the whole picture? Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, could you tell us what is displayed in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is the house to which I was brought when Ivo and Simo brought me to this house here. This is the main road. So it's the third house. It's this house when you go in this direction (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: So when you testified yesterday that you were walked down the main road to Santici and then taken to the third house off the main road, that's the house you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next picture, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, Exhibit 37 has been placed on the machine. It is a photograph of a young man. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is my brother, Muris.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: And he died on the morning of April 16th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've already talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Next picture, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Exhibit 38 depicts a woman. Who is this?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is my mother when she was a girl. I didn't have a recent photograph of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did she survive the attack on Ahmici in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, she didn't. She was killed. She was killed together with my sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us who is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This is my sister, Alma, the youngest. This is she (indicating). And my cousin, Samir, who was also killed on the 16th of April, '93. And this is my relative, she used to live in Vitez, and I don't know who the other two children are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have a -- I believe you testified that when you left the house, your mother and your sisters were still in the house. Do you have a theory as to what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The first thing I heard, on the 17th of April -- I'm sorry, the microphone was off -- as I've already said, I understood that she was still alive, and when Ivo Papic was taking me toward the place in Zume, he told me he had taken my mother and my sisters to the Bosnian lines, and that they had taken two cows and a calf which we had, and I thanked him. However, when I managed to get out into the territory controlled by the Bosniaks, I learned that my mother had not come out of there, and I learned that on the television, CNN report had been shown where Bob Stewart, an English Colonel, said that a woman with her daughters had been killed in a house in Ahmici, and they showed two charred male corpses, and in the translation it said that these are the father and son who are probably trying to protect the mother and daughters who are in the cellar. However, a maniac killed them and then he rushed into the cellar and killed the women and the daughters and threw bombs, and poured gasoline over all this and set it on fire. I think that -- I blame Zoran Kupreskic exclusively for these events, because he was in that area as a kind of commander and he was leading the people in that area. Later on, a commission went to this village, together with UNPROFOR, and they found charred bones. This was then put into bags and buried in Grabovi, in the cemetery as unidentified victims. I know that later on the woman who was killed in Ahmici was not killed together with several of her daughters, but I still believe that this could only have been my mother, based on Colonel Stewart's statement, but Ivo told me that Ivo had taken them there, that he had taken them -- I don't know exactly to which location, and I don't know exactly who he turned them over to. I'm referring to Ivo Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. At this point I would turn the witness over to the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, may I ask you a question? Since the witness has mentioned one or two accused, do you intend to have him identify those particular accused? In particular I'm thinking of Mr. Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I can do that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, do you see Dragan Papic in court here today, the Dragan you have referred to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Papic is sitting in the last row. He has a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think the record should reflect that he has identified Dragan Papic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now turn to Mr. Pavkovic to ask him whether he has consulted with the other legal counsel so that he may tell us who is going to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Pavkovic, I hope you don't mind if each time I turn to you, because you can tell us how many legal counsel are going to cross-examine the witness each time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My colleagues have decided that almost every single one will conduct a cross-examination of Mr. Ahmic. Some of us will do this over a longer period of time and some, if that is necessary, may follow up very briefly, but I would like to announce that all of the Defence counsel will take part in the cross-examination. Of course, taking into account the time that we have available, we will make sure that we do not repeat any questions, but with your permission, I would now like to turn the floor over to Madam Glumac, and she is going to start the cross-examination of Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Glumac

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ahmic, I am Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac. I am Defence counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. I'm going to ask you several questions regarding the events to which you have already testified for the Prosecution, and this is just to clarify certain situations. Let's start with the conflict of 20th October, 1992. Could you please tell us who erected a barricade in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was erected by the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was this barricade erected by the Territorial Defence or by the local villagers? In other words, was this a spontaneous thing, or was there an order?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It came by an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did order this?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This came from the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could that have been Esad Dzananovic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I assume so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know if this man worked for the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why was the barricade erected? What was the basic reason why it had been put up?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It had been erected because, as early as 3.00 in the afternoon, there were -- there was fighting in Novi Travnik. Croats had attacked Bosniaks in Novi Travnik in order to occupy a weapons factory, and I heard the Croat forces were amassing in Kiseljak, Kresovo and they had large forces, and we received orders to prevent them from passing so that they would not go to Novi Travnik to assist people over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who did you receive this information from?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As I already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was this from the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people were manning the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There were only three or four men there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a problem because I don't know how fast--.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you can just wait a few seconds, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: You received information that large forces are on route to Novi Travnik, and this is why you erected the barricade, which only three men were controlling?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were directly on the road controlling it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did it make much sense putting just three men there? Were there additional people there who guarded the barricade who were in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was security around, because not all of them could be on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people did guard the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Not many. I did not count them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How about 20 to 30?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is fair number, 20 to 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were all these men armed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did they expect to offer resistance without weapons if there were all these big forces coming?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: We had to take fighting the way it came to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did you have any trenches next to the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, during the night we dug up some.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you also have trenches in the Catholic cemetery which was nearby?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that we did not have -- I think there were three or four young men from Santici who came, and I believe that they did see that no trenches were dug in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any men in the Catholic cemetery who were guarding the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I do not know that. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: How did this barricade look? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As I said, I did not see this barricade, but I heard that some mines had been laid on the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: But were there also some physical obstacles put?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about these mines? Where did you get these mines from?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They had been brought from the depot at Sljemena which had been destroyed, and somebody had brought them from down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the fall of Sljemena when these barracks were taken, did a number of Bosniaks, that is TO members, did they manage to acquire some arms there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: A lot of these weapons were destroyed. Some had been taken , and the Croats established because they lived in that area. I heard that Croats had taken a lot of weapons away from these people. They had a number of checkpoints there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who attacked this barracks in Sljemena?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know who. I believe that it was a joint attack by the Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who had occupied Sljemena?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in 1992, early '92. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt, but it appears to me that these questions about Sljemena appear to be well outside the scope of direct-examination, and I see no relationship between the direct-examination and these questions on cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you are right, but you know that we have a rule now, Rule 90(H) stating: "Cross-examination shall be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. The Trial Chamber may, in exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into other matters as if on direct-examination." I think we will allow Mrs. Glumac to go on, but with the appeal -- I'll make an appeal that you should confine yourself as much as possible to the facts relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I apologise, but the situation is such that the Prosecution alleges that there were no weapons in the village and that there was no organisation there, and the indictment covers the period including the 20th October until 16 of April of 1993, and this period has been presented in the indictment, so it is in the indictment. All I'm saying is -- all I'm trying to find is how it happened that a certain amount of weapons were accumulated in the village, because the Prosecution alleges that the village had not been armed at all. So I am just responding to the allegations that have been set out in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, you were about to ask questions or raise objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I was actually raising, for clarification from the Court, on the phrase in the Rule "As if on direct-examination." I take that to mean if new subjects are raised on cross-examination, there is a lot of sense in allowing examination at this point rather than having to call the witness back in the Defence case, but I take that phrase to mean that as if on direct the questions must be placed in a non-cross-examination style, that is open-ended questions rather than leading questions as I am used to being permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. In principle I agree with you. However, you may be aware that you put a lot of leading questions, and we were fully aware that many of your questions were leading questions. We thought that we should not object to those questions, because we think, in a bench trial, when there is no jury proper, when there are professional judges, of course, they are able to find out where the -- I mean, to accept and to see whether or not the questions are leading. Therefore, I think it is only proper to take some latitude vis-à-vis the Defence and also allow some leading questions, within, of course, some limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I fully agree some flexibility in that area is good. It speeds things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: But I was asking for clarity for the phrase "As if on direct." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may go on with your questions, but, as I say, please try, as much as possible, to limit yourself to the period relevant to our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell me: Did you have any business or did you work in the communications centre that night between 19th and 20th October 1992?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I was communications person, but that night I was -- I did not work.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you there at all in this communications centre?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That was not a communications centre, it was some kind of a radio transmitter place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That was in the school in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: And that's where you were the communications specialist?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: During that night, did you come to the school at any time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, did I come to the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything over the radio about stopping a vehicle with four HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I did not hear that over the radio. I heard that from people who talked about it. They were talking in a backyard. I heard that four -- four soldiers in the vehicle had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: And who were these people that--?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There were four military policemen and they had been disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Weapons had been taken at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know what type of weapons these were?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: These were, I believe, automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Four automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they returned to these military policemen?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that they had been returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were these the four rifles which -- of which you said that the people from Ahmici were supposed to return to the HVO, condition speaking at time of -- when -- the return of Bosniaks were negotiated?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I was not part of those negotiations. I don't know what happened during these negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you allowed that this may have happened?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many people on your side did take part in this conflict on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That was not a conflict, this was an attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. How many people on your side did defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: With weapons? I believe that there were 30 -- up to 40 people, and without weapons we could not defend ourselves. There were many other people who did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Did anybody else come from elsewhere from the BiH army, from surrounding villages to reinforce your positions?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, some assistance did come.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many people about?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Mostly people without -- who did not have any ammunition, and poorly armed. I can tell that about 50 to 60 people, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: From the direction of Vhrovine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, up to 100 people were defending the village at that time, about 40 to you and 50 to 60 of the others?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, you could say 50 to 60 people, because many people who had come from down there also did not have weapons. So if anybody got killed, they could take the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. But can you tell me, was anybody killed on the Croatian side. You said something about Halid Pezer, but do you have any knowledge about anybody being killed from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I heard a long time has elapsed since, so I heard that some people were killed on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that Andzelko Vidovic from Kiseljak was killed? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know this man, but what is a person from Kiseljak doing there?

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You knew that somebody was coming?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. And people who arrived, arrived from the direction of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: But let me ask you this. Was there fighting going on in Jajce at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jajce had been attacked at that time by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Croats provide assistance to the Muslims in defending Jajce; as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Had the Croats given assistance in Jajce they would not have engaged in this, they would have gone to Jajce to defend it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: But could the Croats have been going in the direction of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was the commander at this barricade, who was making decisions there, whether to remove it or not, who assembled the men?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was my brother Muris.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: He was the TO commander near the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was he at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He probably went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long did the fighting go on that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It went on until, I believe, 2.00 in the afternoon. You could hear fire. And then houses were being set on fire all the way through the dusk.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that after this event at the barricade, your brother Muris was relieved of his duty. Why was he relieved of his duty?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He suffered a shock. I don't know whether he resigned or was removed. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: And Fuad Berbic was assigned to his position?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, it was Midhat, son of Fuad Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus on the period between the two conflicts. Can you just tell me when the Territorial Defence in Ahmici was established?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: In April '92.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in Ahmici was linked to Vitez Territorial Defence or was independent? You said that your headquarters was in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was all linked up regionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the role of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The role of the Territorial Defence was to protect the population which lived in a particular territory. The Territorial Defence had regional headquarters, and it was like we had in our village. It was exclusively to protect the villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were people sent to the front-lines, for instance, in 1929? You already had war with the Serbs. Were they sent from the Territorial Defence to the line?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but these would have been volunteers which volunteered to go there. For instance, Visoko, there was danger that Visoko would have been taken, but these were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what area did the Territorial Defence headquarters of Ahmici cover what was the territory that it covered?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was Ahmici and Santici, and only the Bosniaks were members of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Bosniaks were members of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what types of weapons did they have? Did they have any and how much did they have?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The weapons were of inferior quality and there may have been up to 50 rifles, but when Croats took Zume, they took all the weapons away from the people there, so that maybe up to 20 rifles had remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did the Territorial Defence change its name to army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This was in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was the main staff, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Ahmici, I mean? Who was in command? Did it remain the same? Did they report to Vitez or did the situation change?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The situation did change. It became different but organisationally speaking. This was an initial type of organisation of the army. Some battalions had been established at first, but this was just on paper because there was no equipment and materiel to establish an army or a brigade. I was a member of the battalion at Preocica, but I never went there. I never had any weapons. I never had -- but I was assigned to the Preocica battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: To which brigade did the Ahmici belong?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That was the Vitez brigade. I believe it was 325.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was its command post?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in Vitez or in Kruscica. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did members of the BiH army from your village go to any military training?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There was no -- well, there was sometimes some type of military training in Kruscica or Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the BiH army for Ahmici? (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that was the same commander who had been the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he automatically took over when the army was established. He just remained in his post for our village, to coordinate for the village. But now there were organisational matters regarding the establishment of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether general mobilisation was declared by the Bosniak side and when was that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would like to just ask a couple more questions regarding the village guards. When did the village guards -- when were they established and did they remain in place even after the BH army was established?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The village watches started in the summer of 1992 and Croats also had their own watches. I already testified to that. In the hamlet of Zume, Croats and Muslims had joint watches. They did not have any particular purpose because the war was raging in eastern Bosnia, so this was more in terms of being on alert. However, during the attack in October, after the attack in October, everything changed with respect to Croats. Our own also continued with watches and patrols, especially at night. We were protecting ourselves from any surprises.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did village watches divide, that is, did the Croats man the Croat parts and Muslims the Muslim parts?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I lived in a part of the village where night watches were not allowed at all. The Croats had allowed patrolling, but they only gave them a particular route where they could go, and I'm not sure whether they had allowed them to carry weapons. I doubt it. But in the upper part of the village, the Croats had no control.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean up in Gornji Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there watches in Upper Ahmici as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How about Lower Ahmici? I'm not sure whether I'm giving it the proper name because sometimes it's Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in Krcevine, there were Muslim watches?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say so, but relatively speaking, because they were always under Croatian control. There was mixed population in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that a curfew had been introduced. That did not affect the watches. They continued to keep watch?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was allowed to the people up there, but the part where I had lived in Zume, that is where the curfew was in force.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the curfew in force for the Croats as well? Could the Muslim watch stop a Croat and ask him where he was going in the evening? Did it apply to everyone?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Believe me, in the village where, conditionally speaking, people held watch, I doubt that they were allowed to stop the Croats at any time. I doubt that. In the upper village, they certainly could.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in the upper part of the village, they could stop them, so the curfew applied to the Croats as well there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The Croats had no need to go up there because it was a dead-end street, so to speak. They had no need to go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who determined who was to keep watch, and you didn't say whether the village watches remained at the same time as the army of the B and H was established?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, the village watches -- could you explain the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did this organisation connecting the two village watches remain separate from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did people from the army keep watches or were there village watches?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The village watches were held both by people belonging to the army and by old age pensioners who volunteered to keep watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the situation with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know how the Croats were organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the people who kept the village watches wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, they were dressed in civilian clothes. They had no uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any consequences for those who did not keep -- want to keep watch? Was anyone punished for not doing so?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Rarely. Perhaps, but very rarely, because we didn't have any military police, and I was a witness to events when people said, for example, "I can't keep watch tonight -- or today, I have to go to work." But it was rare.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there a barracks in Ahmici, a place where the people who were members of the army of B and H come back before they went to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, there certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where did these people go when they came home? Where did they stay? Did they stay at home?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were people who lived in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So did they carry their arms with them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps some of them did, but very seldom because arms were required at the front-line in defence against the Serbs, and they couldn't carry their arms because the Croats had checkpoints in Puticevo and other places, so if they had taken their weapons, they would have been taken away in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you say that there were no arms in the village or there were few?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There were few arms in the village, Madam. If there had been a lot of weapons, not so many people would have been killed. There would have been resistance. The Croatian forces were not so superior that they could have taken the village so easily. If we had had weapons, they couldn't have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, did refugees arrive in Ahmici, Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there a lot? Can you give us a figure? You probably know that people arrived.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No -- well, not too many, not too few, the same as everywhere, because there were masses of refugees from eastern Bosnia, Karaula, northern Bosnia, and they were all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were these refugees included in the army of B and H or in the Territorial Defence when they stayed there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Some did and some had to go to their units, like the people who arrived from eastern Bosnia. They would stay for only two days, and then they had to go to the front via Kiseljak. They had to go back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So some joined the Territorial Defence in Ahmici and the army, in B and H, there, and some returned to their homes?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there were two or three people from Prijedor who didn't have anywhere to go, and they kept watch with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have too many questions, but I do have some detail, so I won't be finished very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether you know Safet Imsirovic? Is this name familiar to you, and was he a member of the B and H Territorial Defence, or do you know anything about him? If not, say you don't.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't know Safet Imsirovic. This might be a young man who will take the witness stand, but I didn't know him by name. However, I have heard the surname. I think that this is a young man who will be a witness here, but I didn't know him in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you know a person named Esad Rizanovic in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did they join the Territorial Defence or the army of B and H in Ahmici, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Rifet Buskic (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mujo Rupovic (phoen)?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: No, no. It's not your fault if you don't know them. I'm simply asking whether you know them or not and whether you know whether they were in the army. You said you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I know Rifet, who I think was from the Krajina, but I don't know him by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The situation after the first conflict, when negotiations were held on the return to Ahmici, were these negotiations held at the political or the military level? Who took part in that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I know my brother went to these negotiations and some other people. At what level this was done, I don't know. All I heard was that there had been an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were meetings held at the school?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Fuad Kaknjo (phoen) come there from Vitez; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the Vitez municipality, a decision was reached to help you repair your damaged houses? Did you know that some people had received help?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, some material arrived, but very little arrived. My father got some building material, but a cow shed had been burnt down. We didn't get any roof tiles. The damage was so bad that not enough material was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you did get some help?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did get some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let us now come to the events of the 16th. The two soldiers who came to your house and who took you and your father out to be shot, did they talk about Dusina Zirovic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He said -- I asked him, "What does this mean?" And he said, "What you people have done in Dusina Zirovic?" And I said, "I don't know what happened there." And he said, "You'll know now." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What had happened there? Do you know something about it?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I learned later, after a long time -- I know about Dusina, that certain Croatian units from Busovaca had tried to take the communications point, the cross-roads, and to control the road between Zenica and Sarajevo, and the Bosniak soldiers managed to stop them doing that, and the population from Dusina tried to support the Croatian units and then the Croatian population was driven away, was expelled from Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any civilians, Croats, killed there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I heard that there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know when this happened, how long it was before the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was two or three months before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about these negotiations -- or, no, the talks, sorry, you said that the taller of the two men, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The shorter one. The taller one was searching the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were guarding you in the house into which the bomb had been thrown in the second event, was Busovaca mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they mentioned Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I said that when they arrived by car, the one who was guarding me said, "What's new in Busovaca?" And they said, "Everything is all right." And then he said, "Commander, we have a Mujahedin in prison here." Well, I talked about that, that Busovaca was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you conclude from this that these were soldiers from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: You could say that because when he said to him, "Commander," I presume -- I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let us talk about your movements in the morning, when you came to the drain pipe or the creek -- I don't know exactly what it was -- where you hid. What time was it exactly? Do you know how long it took you to get there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it was maybe half past six, between six and half past six.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you see these units moving into directions as you showed on the map?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was very soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So can you try to be more precise? Was it just after half past six?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Madam, it was in the morning, but I wasn't wearing a watch and I couldn't check it. I can only say it was early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that people wearing various patches arrived, obviously from various units. That's what I understood. Can you tell us the total number of people involved?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think that there were about 80 to 100 men from the north side and 50 to 60 coming from the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was that all at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The ones who came from the north came very soon afterwards, and the ones from the south arrived at various time intervals of about an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "south"?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I mean from the direction of my house. It wasn't the woods, it was a valley, it was from a valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You saw the units, the special units of the HVO, the Vitezovi; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Men in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: These two groups that arrived, did they arrive together or did they arrive separately? I don't mean from the two separate directions, but I mean, did they come unit by unit or did they come together?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The first group, which included civilians, military policemen, it was very diverse. It came and it was close to me. The other group was wearing black uniforms and they were further away from me; and the ones who came from below, in platoon-size units, were exceptionally well-armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone coming down from the direction of Ahmici towards the road or did you only see people leaving while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see anyone coming from the direction of Ahmici. I was in a kind of hole, and I could see only those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, you said that you saw houses burning?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw my house when it was set on fire and a few other houses while I was still on the road. While I was still on the road, I saw houses being burnt. When I went down to the cellar, I saw my house and two other houses bursting into flames.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: For how long could shooting be heard? Until what time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, the shooting, the artillery; I couldn't hear very well because of the noise of the water in the creek. I heard the artillery throughout the day, almost the whole day but at certain time intervals.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have the feeling that there was a battle going on?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you find out or -- rather, until what time did you hear shooting? You said that day until the evening. Did it go on the other day, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: As I told you, I was in the creek, and I couldn't hear the shooting, and the soldiers that ran up, they weren't shooting, they weren't fighting, they were simply preparing. I didn't see any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you hear artillery?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said something about the village of Mahala near Santici. You said yesterday, it wasn't quite clear to me, that there had been artillery shots towards Mahala, but Mahala is inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what reason would the Croats have to shoot at their own village?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I learned later. I didn't know what it was about then, but I learned later that there was an incident in that village so that they were supporting the Croats. They were shooting above the village, not into the village, supporting the Croatian army in the village. I think that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I heard that you also said yesterday, when you were brought to the school in Dubravica, that you had been told that you had to be exchanged for Croats taken prisoner in Poculica; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Nikica Plavcic said that there would be an exchange of prisoners. He brought us to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I interrupt just briefly, and I hate to interrupt this, although I note we're close to the 11.00 hour, but we do have something of a semi-emergency nature to take up I think quickly in closed session, it will not take long, but I think we would request that we do so now. It involves something that happened about 10 or 15 minutes ago on questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, Mrs. Glumac. Probably we should now move into a closed session. If you don't mind, you may continue after the break. So let us now move into closed session for a few minutes and then we will take our break. Thank you. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before I ask Mrs. Glumac to continue with her cross-examination, I had raised an issue and I am grateful to the Registrar for drawing my attention to this issue. I wonder if Mr. Moskowitz intends to tender the various exhibits as evidence so that they're admitted into evidence, the exhibits we have received so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I was intending to do that, although I perhaps was under the misapprehension that merely offering it without objection would be equivalent to the evidence being accepted. I thought I heard that ruling earlier, but maybe I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, no, no. The ruling is that if there is no objection -- whenever a party tenders a document into evidence, then if there is no objection, it is admitted into evidence. But you have to formally say, "I would like to tender this as evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the various exhibits to be regarded as evidence. So far there's been no objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would, at this point, formally tender all of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence counsel object to this, and they do formally object that the documents offered by the Prosecution be tendered into evidence. First of all, we believe that the Prosecutor presented certain photographs on the basis of which it is not possible to determine that they were made in the period of time which is covered by the indictment. So we are -- I don't know if we can enter a discussion on every single exhibit. We would then -- if we did this, we would then be able to tell you individually which exhibits we would accept and which not because some of them simply are not documents of the period of time covered in this indictment, and in particular, they do not refer to individual accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I suggest a practical solution? As far as the documents which have been produced so far are concerned, may I suggest that you and the Prosecutor, you get together maybe at lunch time or in afternoon and agree upon those exhibits which are not objected to by the Defence so that we save time? If there are some documents to which you want to object, then we can maybe pick up this matter maybe tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. But in future, each time a document is tendered by the Prosecutor, you are asked kindly to decide whether or not to object. If you don't object, we take it that you don't object, and they are accepted into evidence. But, as I say, for the time being, let us now avoid a discussion now in court also because I think we are in the process of having a witness cross-examined by Defence counsel, so it would be sort of a digression, it would disrupt the pace of our hearings, and I think it's better if you try to come to some sort of agreement, you and Mr. Moskowitz. Is it fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I accept your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. At the suggestion of Judge May, I would ask the Prosecutor whether he could provide the Court and Defence counsel with a list of the dates on which the various photographs were taken. This might probably facilitate our job and also probably be of some help to the Defence. Later on, of course, in the afternoon or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And before talking with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let us then move on, and I would like to ask Mrs. Glumac to continue with her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MRS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you back to the second conflict and what we talked about before the break. I don't think that we need to go much into detail there, but it seems to me that either in your testimony or in the previous statement, I cannot distinguish between the two now, you saw that Sakib Ahmic's house was the first which was set on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: From the vantage point at which you were, did you also see Sakib Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It is -- that house is a bit more tucked away, but you could see the flames. However, I did refer to Sukrija's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. There are two Sakib Ahmics in Ahmici, and I'm not sure which one she's referring to. So I would ask that a clarification can be made on the question so that the answer can be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, please, when you refer to the Defence counsel, may you use his or her name, not "she" or "he"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As a matter of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest that we somehow have a way of distinguishing between the two Sakib Ahmics. You ask counsel to distinguish. How are we going to distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would suggest that Sakib Ahmic -- there's one Sakib Ahmic who is his uncle and the other Sakib Ahmic is not a relation, not an uncle. So perhaps a reference to "Sakib Ahmic, your uncle," or "Sakib Ahmic, who is not your uncle." You might make that distinction. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So let's use also -- or patronymic. This is Sakib Ahmic to who I'm referring, is the one who lived in middle Ahmici, and his father is Rasid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So Sakib -- Rasid Ahmic. He is farther away from your house. The house of other Sakib Ahmic, your uncle, his father, is who?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Mehmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is the house that is closer to you, it is Lower Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. So from your vantage point, you could have seen Sakib Ahmic's house on fire, but you saw Sukrija Ahmic's house; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a big fire, so I think that Sakib Ahmic's house also was on fire. However, I do say 100 per cent that it was Sukrija Ahmic's house that was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was Meho Rustanovic's house also on fire? Did you see his fire (sic) burning later on as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I cannot speak to that. I believe that this was enough, what I had seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. This is fine. I'm just asking whether you subsequently saw something else. Yesterday you said that from an intersection you saw a truck being off-loaded. These were some crates that were being unloaded in front of Ivica Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: How far is this location from Ivica Kupreskic's house?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe about 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: And this was -- you had a clear view?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, very clear. You could see the house clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you tell me exactly when this took place? Was this earlier or was it the 17th or 18th?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no. This was maybe about a month before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: I see. About a month. In your testimony, you also mentioned the destruction of the lower mosque, that is the -- you said that you saw that on the second day in the evening?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, the second day but at noontime.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Noontime. So you stay by that statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the minaret of this mosque still standing at that time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Only at the moment of the explosion I saw that something was flying. I didn't see whether it was -- I just saw the top of the minaret flying down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that it was destroyed on the second day?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe there was some additional damage done, but I saw the top of the minaret falling.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. How is this part of the village called, the part of the village where you lived? Is that Zume, the part below the road?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: We call it Tuk.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is that part of Ahmici or Zume?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the road which passes between Tuk and Ahmici, you said officially this is Ahmici. Does this road pass through Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this is the road Busovaca-Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you now tell me what is the area of Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Grabovi is the central section of Ahmici, between the Upper and Lower Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where do the Lower Ahmici stop or finish?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: You see, there is no strict line, it is just to facilitate it. There is no particular border or line, strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see. The part that you called Grabovi, how many Croats live there?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The Kupreskic family live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. So Kupreskic. That would be in Grabovi. So that would be at the houses of Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what we called Grabovi. And there's also Zoran's house. Where Zoran's house is, that's already called Pirici, but we called it Grabovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. How many Croats did live there? What is it, five or six Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac, could you please slow down, in particular, wait a few seconds after putting a question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GLUMAC
utterances.text: So five or six Croatian homes would constitute Grabovi. How many people live there approximately? Just approximate numbers.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
