utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sejo Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know about him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Nevsudin Pezer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He was in the police. I think he did have something, a gun.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a hunter. He had a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sefik Pezer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what Sefik had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmed Pezer?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Goran Semir?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Senus Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Senus Pjanic? I don't know whether he had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sabahudin Muratovic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Sabahudin Muratovic? I don't know about him either, whether he had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We are finished with this part. Let us go on. When you said that Zoran was a commander in Grabovi, my colleague asked you how many men there were. In the meantime, you were in the army so that you know about military units, and if you were to put Zoran among the army, would he be the commander of a squad or another size of unit?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: A squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zoran was a guide. Did you see him acting as a guide?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you conclude that he was a guide?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I said I presumed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now we would like to talk about your meeting with Sakib Ahmic. Please try to explain to the Court the television in the part controlled by, let us say, the Muslim side at that time. Was it based exclusively in Sarajevo or was it also in Zenica, Zetel?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think Zetel was based in Zenica only.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: But Sarajevo had a television station as well?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo had a Bosnian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I was unable to follow, so please forgive me, but how many days after the conflict of the 16th of April did you arrive on Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Within eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived on Muslim territory, I presume that it was in the vicinity of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived on Muslim territory, did you have any occasion to see the television programme?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really watch television regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see a television programme about the visit to the victims of Ahmici in the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear about this television programme which was made when the first victims arrived in the Zenica hospital?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know by hearsay or through your own observation that, in this first television programme which was made in the Zenica hospital, Sakib Ahmic, the one who is not your relative, was shown?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that Sakib Ahmic had spoken for the television and some other women as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear what Sakib Ahmic talked about?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't watch the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you didn't watch the programme, you don't know about the details, you only know that it was mentioned on the television. Would you only help me by saying whether this was on Zetel or on the Sarajevo television according to what you have heard?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No one was able to tell me in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Because it's hard for me to identify.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Zenica television.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So it was Zetel. Thank you very much. Let me just ask you about Sakib Ahmic and then we will be done. Can you tell me where you met? I'm not interested in Sakib Ahmic who is your uncle but the other Sakib Ahmic. Where did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: This was in Zenica and we did not sit down, so to speak. We just walked along, so it was a very brief meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could you reproduce this conversation to the extent that it is possible to? Obviously, you did not pay much attention at that time. Everybody had his own worries. But can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He told me that Zoran Kupreskic and Miro broke into the house with weapons, to the house where Naser was and that they killed his wife and his child, that he hid behind some kind of armoire or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Did he describe them, whether they had their faces painted?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. He just told me the main things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: He told you -- did he mention to you that they both were armed with rifles?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they could have had in order to shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. I wonder whether Mr. Moskowitz would like to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I know it's been a long day, so I'll be very brief. You were just asked about your conversation with Sakib Ahmic in Zenica. Could you tell us how Mr. Sakib Ahmic appeared and looked while you were speaking to him? I'm talking about his physical appearance.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: His face was all burned and his arms were also burned, but he had just come out of the hospital so this was all sort of new skin that was growing, both on his face and his forearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Did Sakib Ahmic appear to you to be in some pain as he was talking to you, physical pain?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, certainly. He had been weakened quite a bit and he suffered a lot of pain. He had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked, I believe by Mr. Grospic (sic), about your earlier testimony regarding the October 1992 attack, specifically your testimony about seeing shooting coming out of Ivo and Dragan Papic's house on that day. Do you recall him asking you about that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall one of the Defence lawyers, Mr. Grospic, asking you about your never having said before that you had seen firing coming out of Papic's house on October 22, on October 20th, 1992? Do you recall him asking you about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Since the Prosecution is sometimes raising questions -- I believe that we will need to clarify that Ms. Grospic did not question any witness, and the Prosecutor is referring to Ms. Grospic, and I think he's confusing the witness. I think we need to clarify who it was that posed the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. I hadn't realised that he was referred to Mr. Grospic. Ms. Grospic is the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I apologise. I looked at the wrong name on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Puliselic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: -- suggested to you that you had never spoken before about seeing firing coming from Ivo and Dragan Papic's house. Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that I have said so. Maybe he did not read the statements very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying at the Blaskic trial and testifying on page 3 -- 3724 regarding what you had seen, specifically that firing was coming out of Ivo and Dragan Papic's house that day?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was said in the statements, and I did mention also in the Blaskic case, but I do not -- I do not recall it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked about never having said before to investigators in the Blaskic case about your conversation with Dragan Papic in 1991 regarding Adolf Hitler and those matters. What you were

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: were you specifically asked to give details about Dragan Papic from 1991?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the end, they always asked about the persons who are here now and about some additional persons, whether I knew them, but they only asked very briefly about them, including Dragan Papic. They also asked about him.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Did they ask you to think about anything that you had, any contact you had had with Dragan Papic back in 1991? Did they want you to focus that far back, or were they interested only on the attack in Ahmici in 1993 and how that related to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: In general, they just asked me to mention these people very briefly, but they focused in much more detail on the attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked about the Territorial Defence in Ahmici in 1993, and I'm afraid the suggestion may have been made that the Territorial Defence in Ahmici was, in fact, a military or a highly sophisticated military operation. Was it, in fact, a highly sophisticated military operation in Ahmici in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't say that because there were no conditions for that. We did not have logistics, no war materiel or the military police communications or other facilities needed for the military. There were no uniforms. There was no equipment, supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Bottom line, what was the Territorial Defence in Ahmici in 1993? What was it in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radovic, do you have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This question has been asked and answered. The witness very comprehensively answered that in late 1992, the Territorial Defence became part of the BH army, and so this question has already been asked and answered and I don't think we need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This is not the thrust of my question. Perhaps I need to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you rephrase it probably? Are you asking for a sort of description of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I'm asking for a realistic description of what really was going on in Ahmici in 1993 with regard to the Territorial Defence and not what was going on on paper. What was really happening in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Glumac has an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind -- I would just like to point out that we have already concluded, through the witness's testimony, that in 1993, the Territorial Defence no longer existed. He stated that in late 1992, the Territorial Defence had become the BH army, so now we're going back to something that had been established earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mrs. Glumac is right. I have here in front of me my notes, and the witness said in December '92, the Territorial Defence was incorporated into the army of BiH. I take your point. Thank you. I wonder, Mr. Moskowitz, whether you could maybe again rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Let me put it this way then. The transformation of the Territorial Defence in 1993 to the army, was that, in fact, a transformation that made a difference on the ground in Ahmici or was it just a paper difference?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: There were changes that were both real changes on the ground and on paper. My personal opinion is that by being absorbed into the BH army, the organisation of the Territorial Defence in my village was a bit weakened because people had to go to other front-lines, so we had fewer people. Also, some weapons had to be taken to the front-lines against the Serbs. I can also state now that even elderly men started giving these watches, so that the defence of the village was weakened by this. With the establishment of the army, we did not receive any equipment or material, it was only on paper. But we had no depot so we did not receive anything. So by the establishment of the army and this brigade, I think we were, in effect, weakened.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that basically in 1993, whether you call it the Territorial Defence or the BiH army, in Ahmici it boiled down to several men in civilian clothes walking around the neighbourhood, some armed, some not, at night to protect their homes? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it worked, just as it did during the Territorial Defence period, only it was even weaker now.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Now, you also were asked about all these people who had weapons and that lived in Ahmici. After the attack in 1992, were the Muslims required to turn their weapons over as a condition to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked that all the weapons we possessed be turned in, and they took weapons away in Zume and in Pirici. I don't know how many rifles were there, there were quite a number of them there, and the upper part, the people there refused to turn them in, and then there was the threat we would be attacked. The attack did not take place, there was some negotiations, and then the Croats agreed to have the four rifles that were taken away from them be returned, and I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked, I believe, about the curfew and about how Muslims were stopped by Croat patrols in Lower Ahmici, but that wasn't it possible for Muslim Territorial Defence patrols to stop Croats in Upper Ahmici. Were there any Croats living in Upper Ahmici at all, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Would there be any houses, therefore, for Croat patrols to protect in Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Do you know of any instance whatsoever where a Muslim patrol made up of these civilian homeowners and folks returning from the front, do you know of any occasion at all where they stopped and questioned or detained or disarmed a Croat in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were not, except for the four rifles at the barricade. I don't think that there were any other instances.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: I'm talking about after the barricade, between 1992 and '93?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no. As I said, they did not dare down in the lower village, and Croats never came to the upper village anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: You say they would not dare. Why wouldn't they dare? Why wouldn't the Muslims dare stop the Croats in the lower village and impose a curfew on them and take their weapons away? Why wouldn't they dare?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Because they did not have enough weapons, and they were under constant threat, and rather strong Croat forces had been deployed there in a place called Bungalow, and I also knew that there were soldiers there in some forests around. They had been brought there to assist the Croats. And it is true that in Ahmici they were not very numerous, but they had assistance from people outside.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: In your estimation, Mr. Ahmic, who won the battle in 1992 at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I believe that the Croats won the control of the Vitez/Zenica road, so they won. That was their victory.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: And after the conflict in 1992, really who was in control in Ahmici, was it the majority Muslims or the minority Croats?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The minority Croats, I think you can say, because our only way out to this road was there. You we couldn't go either to Busovaca or Vitez, especially Busovaca. There were checkpoints there. They often would take vehicles away. We were blocked. We had a forest road through Vhrovine. That was the only road out that we had.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: April 16, 1993, who was in control of Ahmici, the majority Muslims or the minority Croats?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: On 16 April, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Who was in control of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: That is when the attack of the Croatian army took place, and they assumed full control over Ahmici and all the population fled, all people who survived.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: On April 15, 1993, do you have an idea about how many Muslims lived in Ahmici and in the neighbouring hamlets like Zume?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Maybe 300 to 400 people.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: That was on April 15th. And how many Muslims do you know lived in Ahmici on April 17th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. On 17 April, I believe that no Muslim was in the village of Ahmici. I don't know about the upper village. I don't know whether they fled on the 16th or the 17th. I heard that they fled in the evening, the night of 16 to 17, so that one could say that on the 17 those who were killed stayed there in the upper village. I know that there was some elderly persons there, several of them, who did not want to leave with those who fled at night. They stayed there and the Croats came in the following morning and killed them, and I believe that even a small child was killed at that time. And probably my mother and my sisters also arrived there on the 17th. So probably on the evening of the 17th there were no Muslims left in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Was Sakib Ahmic, not your uncle, one of the Muslims who left Ahmici on that day? The Sakib Ahmic you talked to in Zenica several weeks later, who was burned?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that he also had fled towards Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: And to best of your knowledge, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, where do they live today?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Their families live in Ahmici and in the hamlet of Pirici, part of Ahmici. That's where their families live.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic's family, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They live in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INVESTIGATORS IN THE
utterances.text: And the ones that didn't survive, where are they?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether any of the victims had been positively identified. I'm not familiar with who of his kin has been identified and buried. I actually don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moskowitz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, how many sisters did you have?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And were they killed on the 16th, all of them?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I assume that they were killed on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How old were they?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Can I say the years of their birth? The oldest one, Smaila, was born in 1969, so she was born in'69. Sabria in 1970, and Alma in 1977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I've got a few questions I would like to ask you, but you must be exhausted, and probably we better take a break so that you can have a rest. We'll take only 15 to 20 minutes, if you don't mind. So I suggest that we now rise and then we come back in 30 minutes. So, say, five to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, if you would assist us on a few areas which are of relevance to this Court? I have two minor and specific questions and two general questions. Let me start with the general questions. First of all, could you explain to us the sort of relations existing prior to probably '92 in Ahmici between the two communities, the Croats and the Muslims? Were members of each community on friendly terms with members of the other community? Did you, say, take part in parties? Did you go, say, to shops, coffee shops together? Did you talk to each other in a friendly way? Was there any animosity between the two groups, say up to '91, early '92?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: No, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And then gradually things changed; is it so?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the first multi-party elections, things began to deteriorate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But before this gradual deterioration, was there any case of intermarriage, for instance, say a Muslim marrying a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. Specifically, I never had an argument with any Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In the Muslim community, was there a particular emphasis on religion? Was there a tradition of, say, a training? Were there many imams? Because we have been told that probably in Ahmici, the Muslim community was particularly strong and focused on religion. Is it so, or what is your feeling? Do you think that there was something which, in a way, distinguished Ahmici from other villages with a Muslim majority?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Imams in Ahmici were no more religious than the Croats in our surroundings. Both were good believers, so to say, but we were not any greater believers than the Croats were. They had masses every Sunday at the cemetery in Ahmici which were well-attended, especially after the fall of Communism, many people entered into religious customs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't make myself clear. I didn't want you to compare the religious attitude of Muslims with that of the Croats in Ahmici. I wanted to you to make a comparison, as it were, between the Muslims in Ahmici and those in other villages, Muslims in other villages. Do you think that there was a particular sort of tendency to be particularly strongly religious in Ahmici so that it was an area, village, where religion, within the Muslim group, did play a major role? Was there any special school for, say, training of imams, or was any particular ceremony ...

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, in that respect, it's a question the Croats have been raising. Ahmici was special because there was a private mosque there. There was an individual who had a lot of money and he built a mosque. We saw that in a photograph. And this man gave a lot of money for the building of a mosque. So Ahmici was special because this mosque was built, which was a kind of extra mosque, so to say, but this man had a lot of money, and he decided to build a mosque. So it made things look as if people were more religious. And, as I said, after the fall of Communism, in the Muslim community, people turned to religion to a greater extent. You might say that this did take place. But Ahmici was special because there was this private mosque there, and this attracted attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. I move to a different question. I think you said that prior to December '92, only Bosniaks were members of the Territorial Defence in Ahmici. Did I understand you correctly? Only, I think at one point you said that the Defence, the Territorial Defence in Ahmici, consisted only of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why, why was it so. Because, in a way, Ahmici was a village consisting of a majority of Muslims and a minority of Croats. Now, we are talking about '92, say from January up to, say, December '92. How do you explain that no Croats were members of the Territorial Defence? Can you think of any reason?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: The Croats had established a military organisation long before we did because there was a war in Croatia, and they transferred the military structure to Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were better organised. And we started establishing our Territorial Defence as best we knew how while the Croats already had weapons and they had already experienced a war in Croatia, because young men from our vicinity went to fight in Croatia, and they had their strategy probably not to enter the Territorial Defence. They already had a well-established institution, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So therefore there was a sort of split along ethnic and religious lines between the Croats and Muslims -- when did this sort of split occur in '92, or was it in '92 or '91? When did you set up the Territorial Defence consisting only of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: It was in 1992. In April '92, we established the Territorial Defence. I think the Croats had established the Croatian Defence Council earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move to minor and specific questions. There was an episode you told us about which is interesting and also puzzling. You mentioned that at one point, I think it was on the 16th of April, you heard two Croats talking, and the senior Croat told the junior Croat to execute the orders, and this was said to him three times and he refused to do so. I assume these were orders to shoot at civilians, probably. Now, could you tell us -- this is what I can infer from what you said. Now, were those two soldiers wearing uniforms, and if so, what sort of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage military uniforms and they were painted, their faces were painted in different colours, and they had automatic guns, automatic rifles, with the part that you hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did you see whether there were any insignia, whether they were wearing any insignia, and what sort of rank the senior or older soldier had?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: They didn't have any insignia, they only had blue ribbons, blue bands, on their right shoulder, and they had probably taken their patches off, and I didn't see any ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: What is your guess? Did you at that stage, at that particular time, think of the place from where they probably came or whether they belonged to Ahmici or to a group stationed elsewhere or coming from other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could you think of that particular stage of sort of their, I would call it, origin? Sometimes you can say, judging from the language or the sort of accent somebody speaks, you can say this person comes from that particular village or area or region. Could you make an inference at that particular time, point in time?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: I may have mentioned in my statements, I assumed that the tall man was from Herzegovina and that the younger one was from Busovaca. As far as I can remember, I had even seen him on several occasions in a disco in Busovaca called the Butterfly, and I assume he was from the village called Buselji, which is near, up there, and I had seen him earlier in the disco. It's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But did you conclude that they were regular members of the HVO, professional soldiers, I mean, or members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably they were because they had strict orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: My final question is a minor one. It's about your wound. I think you said that you were taken to a hospital, you went to a hospital about six, seven, or eight days after you were wounded, after the 16th of April, '93. You were probably visited and examined and treated by a doctor, by a medical doctor, at that hospital. If this is so, did the doctor explain to you why, how it came about that, although you were shot at close range, you had not even fainted? Did you get an explanation for this strange phenomenon, which is quite usual, and luckily so. Did you get an explanation? Did he explain to you how it had come about?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: He said to me, it's like when you put a thread into a needle, that's how the bullet passed through, so it didn't damage any of the major bones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Did he find it quite normal that you had not even fainted but you had recovered immediately and you had been able to actually run away and spend a whole day in the ditch, I mean, in water? Yes? Did he explain this to you?

utterances.speaker: ABDULAH AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the x-ray showed that the bullet had passed only through the minor, small bones, and he was convinced that that's why I had fared so well and why I hadn't fainted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I think I had a few more questions, but they are not important, and I assume you are really now exhausted, so I think you should go home and have a rest. Is there any objection to our witness being released? I see none. Mr. Ahmic, thank you so much for coming here to court to testify. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, will you now call your next witness? Oh, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is Mr. Esad Rizvanovic. He's place number 6 in the list of witnesses which was handed over to you on the 3rd of August. The reason why we call him today is that we have some concerns. His wife is in Bosnia, she is paralysed, she needs constant treatment and care, and we made a commitment to him not to delay him overduly here in The Hague, so that's why we asked him to be called as soon as possible. Mr. Rizvanovic wanted to have some protective measures, face distortion, and the Defence shows agreement to this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So no pseudonym, only face distortion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, we have to bring close the blinds. While we are waiting for the witness, may I draw the attention of the parties to our guidelines? I wonder whether you have kept those two pages, the guidelines? Please, don't -- if you need more copies of the guidelines, please tell us, because we attach great importance to our guidelines. My colleagues rightly pointed out to me that we should not forget what is stated in Guideline number C-1, where we stated: "The order of examination and cross-examination will follow the order in which the accused are listed on the indictment." Now, that means that we would like now to stick to this particular guideline and ask now, in this case, the Defence, but this will apply, of course, to the Prosecution as well in any other case, ask the Defence to follow this order. So therefore, we assume that the witness each time should be cross-examined by legal counsel according to the list of accused. So we would start with Mr. Radovic and then -- yes, Mr. Pavkovic? Yes. I think you had ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to inform you that the Defence counsel do not have these guidelines. It must be some kind of administrative error. So I would like to ask the Court that we may be given copies of these guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, on the 15th of May, we mentioned those guidelines, and I think I read them out, so therefore, they can even be found in the transcript. However, however, it is very easy now to make photocopies of those guidelines, and we will provide you with a copy. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We respect the guidelines of the Court and the desire of the Court for us to speak in the proper order. However, the Defence counsel have agreed in principle and we would like to ask you to accept this principle, that the first Defence counsel to start the cross-examination should be the one who finds the witness most pertinent to his client and then we may proceed in the order stated in the guidelines. I think that this is a very practical solution because this Defence counsel will be the one to have the most questions to ask, so I would like to ask you to accept this principle which will alter the guidelines a little bit but not materially. However, we agree in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Yes, to my mind, it's quite sensible. So we would then start with the legal counsel who feels that his client is the most directly concerned and then we will follow the order as stated in our guideline. All right. I think that's a good compromise, and we thank you. We will now move on to our next witness, if he is nearby. Yes, you mentioned Mr. Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, sometimes there are some spelling errors, but he is indeed called Rizvanovic with an R-I-Z-V-A-N-O-V-I-C. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, good afternoon. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: May it please the Court ... Mr. Rizvanovic, your first name is Esad?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In 1993, you were nearly 50 years old. You're married and you have one daughter?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You were born in the area of Prijedor. You were driven away from the area of Prijedor after fighting with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you came to settle in the area of Ahmici. What time did you settle in the area of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In which month?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I think it was in October. No, I apologise. I left Prijedor on the 22nd of August, so it was sometime in September. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which you found some place to live in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Since I was in Travnik and there was no place there, I spent a little while there. Then I went to Vitez, and I was at a children's holiday centre for two days. Then this village accepted us who were refugees, and we arrived here and we were received by Hidajet Bilic. He took us into his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So Mr. Bilic made a house available to you; it was a house which he didn't occupy?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: He was where we were, together, the whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to show a photograph, an aerial photograph, to Mr. Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you please turn the photograph around on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, is it possible for the Judges to have the photos at the same time so that we can follow? Which is the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, can you see the photograph on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: It isn't switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, do you recognise the specific neighbourhood in Ahmici on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Please help me by pointing out the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The upper part of this photograph shows the Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: It's here, and this would be the road leading down and this was the weekend house where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It might be better, Mr. Rizvanovic, if you showed the area on the actual photograph.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This is the cemetery, this is the road, and this is the weekend house where I was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, this means that the houses to be seen within the white circle on this photograph show the house where you settled, which was made available to you when you arrived in Ahmici in September 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This was later, this was Djula's house, and this, near the mosque, was his house, and then later I moved to the weekend house. Where's the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, the house I am now interested in is the house where you settled with your family when you arrived in Ahmici in September 1992, and it is indeed the house that is located within the white circle close to the Catholic cemetery --

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was later. That was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, can you explain to us what that house represented that is located within that white circle in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This should be the weekend house of Djulaga Sarajlic below the cemetery which I occupied later, and up here next to the mosque, or near the mosque, but I can't find the mosque here, this was where Bilic's house was, and I stayed with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The mosque is in the lower right part -- or the lower part of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Oh, here is the Bilic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you mark, with a cross, the house where Mr. Hidajet Bilic is? Can you see the mosque? Take your time. Mr. Rizvanovic, you are now pointing to the main road between Vitez -- Mr. President, would you allow me to help the witness locate the mosque? That's the mosque. Yes, you can see the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the Prosecutor is going to testify on witness's behalf, then we don't need the witness. Could the Prosecutor please refrain from doing this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, the Prosecutor asked me whether he was allowed to, and I said yes. I guess that the witness knows perfectly well where the mosque is. That's not that essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The Defence counsel is aware of the problems faced by the witness in explaining what happened. The Defence counsel is perfectly aware of the situation. Emotions can make things a bit difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you mark it, with a cross?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Here. This is the house of Mr. Hidajet Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, during the late 1992 and early 1993, you were residing in Ahmici. Did you get to know people living in the neighbourhood of the places where you yourself stayed?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I knew several houses surrounding the Bilic house. There were Muslim houses, and then I also knew -- vaguely knew some other houses, and then farther up I did not go very much, so I did not know anybody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you name some neighbours residing in Ahmici? Could you still name them today?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Well, there were -- let me see. Munir Ahmic. I forgot his father's name. I also know Nedzib. His last name as also Ahmic. I also knew Nezir. I don't know his last name, but he had a house over there, and let me see who else. These houses more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You have just named a few people. All these people are or were of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You yourself are of Muslim faith; aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you get to know, at the time, Croat residents in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I never met them, but I know the Papic house. There were others there, but I did not come to know any of them down there in this settlement where there were all these weekend houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where was the Papic house located?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Papic's house was when you go from the cemetery up. I knew that house because I passed it often, and then on the other side there were also some Catholic houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, because I passed by there frequently and I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What impression did you gain from seeing Mr. Papic?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I once was going to a village down this road, and there was somebody else with me, a neighbour, and we were walking up this road to go to the village, and I saw him wearing black clothes, and I saw him with a sniper rifle and a hat on his head, and we just passed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Would you be able to describe a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: It's a rifle which has this optical instrument. How do you call that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did this encounter take place? Could you locate it in time to the best of your memory?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This was before the trouble, several days before it. I don't know exactly the date. This was when we passed by, so that was around that time. He walked past us, we walked past him, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your answer, Mr. Rizvanovic. When did you see Mr. Papic dressed in that way?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Oh, that. That was -- I didn't have a watch, but it was in the afternoon hours, more towards the dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And do you remember in which month this took place, this encounter took place?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This was before this trouble, before the attack on Ahmici, and this attack on Ahmici took place on 16 April. So this was several days before this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Had you met Mr. Dragan Papic on several occasions, or was that occasion which you have just described the only occasion?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I just walked by. When I would go in to Vitez I would pass by his house, and I would just kind of glance over, and that's when I saw him. He was walking in the direction of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you see him on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I saw him that one time, but, otherwise, I would just see him like that. It was also a long time ago. I saw him once in front of his house. He was standing there. He was there with another two friends of his, and they had some kind of automatic rifles. I didn't pay much attention to that, I just passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And was he dressed in uniform?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And could you describe that uniform? What kind of uniform was that?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Black, black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Papic's house was along the road which you often took to go to Vitez. Now, did the house stand out in any way, in any special way?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes. It had two flags. One was a chequer-board flag and one was a black flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And you personally saw the two flags, the chequered flag and the black flag from the house -- on the house of Dragan Papic; did you?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This was flown from the windows. One was small, and the chequer-board one was fairly long. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When did you notice those flags flowing or hanging from the house of Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: When in 1992 or 1993 did you notice that there were flags, a black flag and a chequer-board flag, on the house of Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: They were flying there all day long. I don't think that he would take them down over the night too, they were there all day long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And the fact that the flags were there was such that that house stood out somehow in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I don't know how it stood out. You mean that the other houses did not have flags and this one did? I'm not clear on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's perfectly right. Did the other Croat houses have flags as well?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I did not see that. There were a lot of chequer-board flags around, and as far as the other ones are concerned, I did not pay much attention. Whenever I passed by, I would sort of keep my eyes down so that I would not be catching anybody's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And why were you afraid when you would pass those specific houses?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Well, you know, I barely survived over there, and here it wasn't very good either. You could see that because of the shooting, and then at night there was a lot of shooting going on in the forest, and things were being thrown on the road, so I don't know, I was afraid. It was similar to how it was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you mean that the feeling of insecurity and lack of safety that you had in Prijedor, which forced you to leave Prijedor, was present and was the same, was as vivid as it was then in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same, and I was afraid, I was quite afraid, because if you throw devices, if you shoot around forests, of course you will be afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you see a lot of black uniforms in Ahmici prior to the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: They moved around, for the most part. It depended, and most of them were black uniforms. There were a few of those others -- how shall I call them -- those camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yeah. Would you call them camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't understand you well. Could you repeat it? You know, the camouflage, a little bit green and a little bit red, green again. You know, just like the armies wear now, but for the most part they were wearing black things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that other inhabitants, I mean inhabitants of Ahmici, other than Dragan Papic, I'm talking about those people who lived there together with their families, but other people living in the village would wear black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I could not distinguish among them. When they would pass by there, they would put some paint on them or dark glasses or hats so you couldn't make out who was who.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, I'll ask you to turn to the photograph again, the one which is on your monitor. Take your time, do not hurry, and please show and circle with a circle the house of Dragan Papic. You can take your time. I think now you've found your bearings on this photograph, so try and find the house.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Oh, it's hard for me to orient myself here on these photographs. This is the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you see the main road -- or rather the Catholic cemetery, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I see it here. And then this is the road going up to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's it. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: So this is the cemetery. So somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now, do you want to draw a circle around the place where, to the best of your memory and your ability to orient yourself on this photograph, can you draw a circle around the house of Dragan Papic?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: This is our road, and this was this settlement, and this would be somewhere up here, so I think it would be maybe here, around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Well, if this -- you know, the best you can do, just draw a circle in red around the place.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: So this was some distance away from the cemetery, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is fine. Yes. The Court will be pleased with that. Let us move to another question, Mr. Rizvanovic. You answered such a question when you were interviewed by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor. You then said that in the evening of the 15th -- in the evening or the afternoon of the 15th of April, '93, you had noticed some unusual, strange movement in the village. Could you elaborate on that? Could you tell us what you noticed on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the first we ever know here that this witness has talked to anybody in the Office of the Prosecution, because we only received a statement which -- from the Prosecution which this witness gave to the security services of Bosnia. So if the Prosecution has a statement given by this witness, I request that we interrupt this examination, that a statement be turned over to us and that this witness be recalled in 48 hours, or within a month as some of my colleagues suggest. The only thing that we have is the statement which was given to the Agency for Investigation and Documentation in Sanski Most, and we had agreed that this witness is examined based on this statement, but if they have anything else, we first need to see it before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may reassure the Defence counsel so that we put an end to this question. I made a mistake, and I do apologise to the Court and to the Defence counsel. I did not mean investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. There were, indeed, investigators from Bosnia who took a statement on the 7th of May, 1998. It was taken by Mr. Ibric and signed by Mr. Rizvanovic. This is the only statement we have. It was disclosed to the Defence on the 30th of June. Therefore, in keeping in your decision of last Monday, there is no objection, no inconvenience to us going into this matter today. I can reassure the Defence counsel this is the only statement we have. We have no other statement that would have been provided by Mr. Rizvanovic, or I have no statement relating to Mr. Rizvanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you were mentioning this very document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Indeed, the one drawn up on the 7th of May, 1998, from the Agency for the Investigation and Documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac, is everything fine?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, we were speaking of the somewhat unusual events that you witnessed in Ahmici towards the end of the day on the 15th of April, 1993. Could you recount them to us?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On 15 April, in general, every morning I would get up and I would look outside to see what the -- what was happening on the road to Vitez and Busovaca. It was sort of an observation post that I established there. If there were vehicles passing through, I considered that a good sign. On the Thursday to Friday, everything became a bit suspicious to me. First of all, that there was some kind of traffic, increased traffic, going towards Busovaca. I see that there were more people around, and my weekend house had an upper floor, and if I couldn't see well, I would climb up there, and I looked out, and there were these vehicles moving about back and forth. After dusk, I saw that the Catholics who were there with us. I know that women always were busy, about housework and such. I also saw that there were no children or women around. I saw some men in uniforms, they were walking around, and I told my wife and to my daughter, "Something is not right, because nobody is around." They had been taking their people out to Busovaca and to Vitez, women and children. So when I figured this out, I saw that the houses were empty, there were only those in which refugees were staying were inhabited, and I said to my wife and daughter, "We're not staying here tonight." And I first told my daughters, "Go up the road and through the village to the Bilic place." And then I said to my wife, "You will later go and join her at Bilic's, because we had initially stayed at Bilic's and he was a wonderful man. And I told them, "I will follow you later." So later when I wanted to go, there was this man after with me. I believe his name was Brkan, Bruchan or something. He was also a refugee. And there was also Fahim, and he was from Tjentiste, from that area. And I called him up and I said, "Do you see this? Everything is empty. This is not good." So Avdo smiled and he said, "I don't know which houses." I said wherever you go, you should go because nobody will chase you away there because there's nobody there. So I told him this and I left and I went up to the Bilic's place and that's where I stayed for the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, this means that in the evening of the 15th of April you moved from the house where you were staying until then, and you went to the --

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, to the Bilic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Because you didn't feel safe, you were afraid; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: That's right, that's right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: To clarify this question related to the houses, it wasn't very clear before, would you mind taking the pointer and showing -- you can see the sort of TV aerial-like pointer next to you?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: You mean the Catholic ones? You mean the Catholic ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Rizvanovic, that's not what I mean. I'll ask you to point to the house where you were before you moved to the Bilic house. And I'll ask you to show whether it is from that house that you noted unusual movement and when you felt that you were no longer safe.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I was here in this house belonging to Djulaga Sarajlic. This was the first weekend house, right next to the forest. That's the weekend house where I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This is the house that has a white circle on the photograph, the one with the white circle around it on the photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Here on the left-hand side here it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rizvanovic. So this is the house from which you made observations that you described. You saw the people leaving, the house being emptied out, all the locations where there usually were women and children, and where, on that day, on that evening, there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this is the house, which you've just pointed out, the house with the white circle around it, from which you made the observation of the strange movement on that night?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On that occasion, did you see Croat families leaving the village?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: That's exactly what I noticed, that the village was being emptied. They used vehicles and everything, and they were transferring their families both in the direction of Vitez and Busovaca. And in the evening I climbed to the top of my weekend house, I looked around, there was nothing there. Under normal circumstances, women would be working around the house, and they would go about their business, and that night, I could only see a few persons in uniforms, and I told my wife, and then later to the others, that things are not good and there will be some trouble, and that's what happened on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, given this situation of fear in which you were on the 15th, on the basis of what you saw, you decided to go to the Bilic house in order to be in a safer place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bilic's house is the house which you showed earlier on and which you marked with a cross on the photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So the house is close to the mosque, to the mosque with the minaret?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, could you tell us what you noticed in the morning or in the early morning of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: The night when I arrived in Bilics' house there was another person there and I told them that things were not good, because if you looked down from Bilics' house, as it was growing dark, you could see that everything was quiet. There was no movement on the road. A friend arrived from Vitez who worked in a bakery owned by a Croat man, and he said that he was going past some checkpoints and he said that they were all armed, that they were wearing helmets, that from Vitez all the way to Ahmici, it was all like that. So I did not -- I couldn't sleep that night, and also I didn't let my wife and daughter sleep, and I think that that was the same situation with the Bilics'. They had one room, we had another one. So I kept controlling the situation, I kept controlling the road, because I was really focused on the road, and it was sometime around 5.00, 5.30, I was -- I had been awake all night. I was very afraid, I was concerned. That's when I heard the first shot coming from up above, and it was a rifle shot, and that, I believe, was some kind of a signal. Then I took my wife and my daughter and told them to get up, and they asked, "What happened?" And they said, "I heard a shot." And a moment later, from that upper side, I think that the sniper fire started and then everybody got up, the Bilics and everybody else, and from that side, the shooting increased. Bullets flew like bees. So we went down, and that's where we were when it started spreading around the village, and then it started like cross-fire and then larger weapons started appearing; and from Bilics' house, we crawled. When the fire would subside, then we would lie still. And then little by little, we went to place owned by Sreten Nedzib, like some kind of a basement, and we barely made it there because the fire was very heavy, because we were in some kind of a horseshoe there, and we were there in this basement for a long time. There were some wounded people there. There was a lot of shooting. Some managed to flee, but we stayed in this basement. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, you can go on, Mr. Rizvanovic, but beforehand, I would like to come back to one point in your statement. You testified that you were awake because you hadn't slept all night. When you heard the first shot, and as you can remember, there is no doubt whatsoever you heard a first shot before any other shots, and you said that you felt like it was a signal, as if it was the signal to launch the offensive or the assault -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Well, I imagine it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The first shot, so you thought it was a signal. I mean, that was your personal opinion, of course.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you indicate -- sorry, going back to the photograph -- but could you indicate on the photograph at which exact location you were when the first shot was fired? Were you in the Bilics' house? Were you outside the house?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I was in Bilics' house in the kitchen, and the kitchen was facing toward the upper side. I was in the kitchen of the house opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Was it the first floor?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the first floor. My wife and I were in the kitchen, and he and his family were in the other rooms, and this is where the three of us were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So the three were you yourself, your wife, and your daughter?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You said that this first shot and the ensuing shots were coming from the upper village. What do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: There's a cellar and it's this side, the point where the Croatian houses were. They had a cellar on that side over there, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be very accurate, Mr. Rizvanovic, because this is important testimony, and you say that the very first shots --

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, it came from that side, on the upper side, from up above. There was the mosque, and that's where we were, and that's the direction it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. Rizvanovic? What do you mean by the upper part? Based on the place where you were, in the Bilics' house, so you're not far from the mosque with the minaret. So what do you mean by the upper part? Where did the shots come from? Where were the snipers, the shooters? Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I only say it came from the upper part of the mosque where Sutre is, that side, where Kupreskics were, on that side. That's where the first bullet came from, and then even stronger bullets came from that side towards us. And then cross-fire started because it started to surround us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Terrier. It's ten past five. I suppose that you have a lot of questions to ask of the witness. Do you want to finish for the day on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, so I could be finished in ten minutes for the examination-in-chief. I do not want to mention other aspects of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, ten minutes, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shall endeavour to complete the examination-in-chief within ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall tender Exhibit number 40 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, you now can see a photograph of the upper part of the village in relation to the area or the place where you were, that is in Bilics' house; that is in the very centre of this photograph. You have a parking area, the Sutre parking area. Can you see this white spot in the middle of photograph?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you can see that white spot in the middle of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Only it's bigger than it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned Croat houses in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes. These were, you see, these were their houses and those were the Muslim houses around here, but these houses here were their houses, and then over here, on that side, there were some Croatian houses, on this side here too. This road leading here, those were their houses. There were a lot of Croats there also. And then this road leading up --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Pardon me for interrupting, but how do you designate the Croat houses in Sutre?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I used to pass by, and I would pass by on the other side too, and I know that those people who were here, that those were Catholic houses around this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question, Mr. Rizvanovic. How did you usually name those Croat houses? What name did you give them?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I don't know what I would call them. Houses are houses. What can I say? And this was a cellar down here where there was a shop, and it was around here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, when you gave the statement I mentioned earlier on, which was disclosed to the Defence on the 30th of June, you mentioned the house of Vlatko and Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic's houses. You mentioned some fire, some shooting from that direction. Do you remember that statement you made then? And is this in keeping with the memory you have of the events of the time?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: I know I gave that statement. That's what I say. They were up here near the mosque and they shot from up there where their houses were. From Kupreskics' house, they shot down toward the mosque and towards us, from Zlatko and Vlatko Kupreskic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What you are telling us is that, as far as you can remember, the first shot was fired, which seems to be a signal, and then the first shots fired during that assault on the 16th of April, 1993, were fired from the Kupreskic houses in that Sutre neighbourhood, and all this was noticed by you from the house of Bilic where you were, the house being close to the mosque; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: It was -- that's when it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour, this is really leading the witness. There is no point to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have an objection to this examination. The witness doesn't know what to say. The Prosecutor is suggesting what he should say. The first statement was taken six years after the event. He seems not to have understood it, and the Prosecutor is asking him in a leading way. We really believe this is not a proper way to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, could you try to formulate your questions in a different way which would not be a leading way, not suggesting the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. I did not intend to ask a leading question, but I shall take due account of your remarks and put the questions in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanovic, you're telling the Court that you clearly heard the first shot fired during the attack. It doesn't matter whether it was a signal or not, but that was the first shot fired, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You heard it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. I didn't sleep all night, so I heard it, and it was at that time when the attack started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, in relation to you, to where you were, where did the first shot come from?

utterances.speaker: Esad Rizvanovic
utterances.text: It came from the direction of the Kupreskics' houses, up there. This is the cellar, and from there, the fire came at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This question, where the first shot came from, has been asked by the Prosecution five times. This is the sixth time. I think there is no point to this, and I think we should finally end this question of where the first shot came from. If the witness doesn't give him the answer he wants, it doesn't mean he can ask him the same question six or seven times until he gets the answer he wants to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Radovic. I think you're right. Yes, the question was asked several times by the Prosecutor and it was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked the question in the way which you deemed appropriate. I thought that the witness answered adequately, and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you're finished with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned, and we shall reconvene as usual at 9.30 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
